messages.author: 343fd12501b7fca4
messages.subject: Irregular gaps in GPS data
parts:
Hi Chris,

Just discovered the package and am really excited to explore it. Very happy to see the level of support you are providing.

I am working with bobcat GPS data from Iridium collars. The collars missed many Iridium transmissions leading to missing chunks of data ranging from a few hours to several days, randomly interspersed throughout the collection period of 6-8 months. I see it is possible to account for variable fix intervals, which we also have, but I am wondering if it is possible to account for these random gaps. In some other movement models I have used it has been possible to set a maximum time lag to incorporate into analysis, is that an option here?

Below are variograms for 9 of the bobcats. I'm wondering if the abovementioned data gaps could be contributing to the wide undulations in the semi-variance.
Side-note- I see a couple of the cats are not exhibiting range residence. This seems like a very effective method of determining transiency vs residency, or detecting range shifts. Cool!

Thanks,
Dave

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Irregular gaps in GPS data
parts:
Hi Dave,

One of the major benefits of working in continuous time is that irregular sampling is not necessarily problematic. In ctmm.fit() the missing times are properly marginalized over. In akde() there is the weights option to account for irregularity (https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/eap.1704).

The variograms are more sensitive to irregularity (though they are only for visualization), and there are options for dealing with this: dt, res, and fast.

Overall, your variograms look pretty good and its hard for me to say exactly what your gaps are doing without knowing the autocorrelation structure of the gaps, but I don't think uncorrelated, short gaps will cause any major artifacts in the variograms. You can always simulate data with the same sampling schedule to see what impact there is on a known truth.

Bobcat #4 looks dispersive (male?). Bobcat #9 looks like they have a lunar cycle of some kind.

Best,
Chris

messages.author: 343fd12501b7fca4
messages.subject: Re: Irregular gaps in GPS data
parts:
Thanks for the quick response Chris,

That is great. I am really digging this approach. I've worked through the package successfully for a couple cats and it is very user friendly.

Bobcat #4 is a male and appeared to exhibit very stable range residency from February to June, then suddenly dispersed a very short distance immediately adjacent to his former range.

Bobcat #9 is an interesting case. Also male, he exhibited a bimodal home range that appeared stable upon visual inspection of the data. It's only just now that I am seeing this cycling back and forth, something I will definitely need to put more thought into. In your opinion, is it practical to fit a model to his data?

Best,
Dave

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Irregular gaps in GPS data
parts:
Hi Dave,

There are periodic models in the package that you can fit to the data (https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/articles/periodogram.html). I just recently got the model selection working for them. I imagine a lunar periodicity would be resolved in Bobcat #9.
simulate(), speed(), predict(), occurrence(), ... should all work for these models, but home-range estimation is not yet coded for non-stationarity (something might come out of the function, but its wrong). The bandwidth optimization is computationally much trickier for the non-stationary models.

Best,
Chris

PS: You can segment Bobcat #4 and estimate the two ranges. The segmented variograms should asymptote as a check.
